title: Sariputra transformed
hook: the goddess switches bodies with Sariputra to show that male and female are not fixed

segments.voice: Yesterday, heavenly flowers slid off the bodhisattvas and clung to the disciples who called them improper. Your line: the flowers stick.

Shariputra is still sitting there with petals on his robe, and he has a question for the goddess. She's clearly wise; she's just out-talked him about the flowers. So he asks: why don't you change out of your female form? Some readers hear behind it an old view that certain attainments weren't open to a woman as a woman. To him, the question sounds reasonable. The goddess answers it twice: once with words, and once with his own body.
screen: `PETALS STILL ON HIS ROBE.` → `WHY NOT CHANGE YOUR FORM?` → `SHE ANSWERS TWICE.`

segments.voice: First the words, paraphrased. I've looked for the marks of being female, she says, and I haven't found them. So what would I change? Suppose a magician conjures up a woman. Would you ask the illusion to change her form? No, says Shariputra; an illusion has no fixed form to change. Just so, says the goddess. Nothing has a fixed form. Then the second answer. By her power, she turns Shariputra into a likeness of herself, and herself into a likeness of Shariputra. Now the goddess, in his form, asks Shariputra, in hers: why don't you change out of your female form? Bewildered, he answers: I don't know how I turned into this. If you could change out of it, she says, then everyone in a woman's form could change. You aren't a woman, yet you appear as one. In the same way, all who appear as women aren't women in some fixed, final way. The Buddha taught that all things are neither male nor female. Then she lets him go back. Where is your female form now, she asks. It isn't anywhere, and it isn't nowhere, says Shariputra. That's how it is with all things, she says. Afterward Vimalakirti tells him this goddess has served many Buddhas and can take whatever birth she wishes. A few weeks ago, the Lotus had the dragon king's daughter changing form to make a point. Here the question is turned around on the one asking it. The label he was sure of turns out not to be fixed.
screen: `I'VE LOOKED, AND FOUND NO MARKS.` · `A MAGICIAN'S ILLUSION.` · `I DON'T KNOW HOW I TURNED INTO THIS.` · `NEITHER MALE NOR FEMALE.` · then, large: `NOT FIXED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a label you wear, or one you've put on someone: the shy one, the difficult one, too old for that. Ask what the goddess asked: where exactly is it? Look for where it begins and ends, and notice whether it's as solid as it sounded.
Sariputra transformed. The goddess swaps forms with him to show that male and female aren't fixed, and asks why he doesn't change back. Today's word.
Your line: not fixed. Even the one asking the question can change shape. Day eleven ninety-one.

howItsDone: Mahayana teachers read the goddess's exchange with Shariputra as a lesson on emptiness, that no form is fixed, and some modern Buddhist writers also draw on it in discussions of women in Buddhism.

chat.says: Why does the goddess turn Shariputra into a woman? Is it a punishment?
options: No, it shows him male and female aren't fixed forms; his own label turns out not to be fixed.
Yes, it punishes him for being rude about her flowers, and she keeps him that way for good.
No, she wants to prove that women are always wiser than monks, so he should stay a woman.
chat.meaning: The goddess swaps their forms to show that nothing has a fixed form: all things, the Buddha taught, are neither male nor female.

Shariputra.meaning: a great disciple of the Buddha, known for wisdom

Vimalakirti.meaning: the wise householder of Vaishali at the center of this sutra
